cards.text: Elihu, the young man who waited his turn to speak (Job 32:4, 6), has been talking to Job. Now he keeps going and turns to a new crowd: wise men, men of learning. Baker, this man waited a LONG time for the floor, and he is NOT giving it back.

cards.question: Elihu wants the wise men to give his words a real test. He says the ear tests words the way the mouth does what?

cards.text: Baker, I taste-test every batch before it goes in a box. Some of MY old lines? Straight to the crumb pile. Didn't even make it to the cooling rack.

cards.question: True or false: Elihu tells the wise men to sort out what is right on their own, without him.

cards.text: Now Elihu brings up Job by name, and he quotes what he says Job has declared.

cards.question: What does Elihu say Job has declared?

answers.text: He is righteous but God denied him justice
He sinned and earned all his suffering
His friends are the ones who wronged him

cards.text: Elihu keeps quoting Job: 'Would I lie about my case? My wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.'
Then Elihu asks, 'What man is like Job, who drinks up derision like water?' Baker, that is NOT a compliment you frame and hang up in the bakery.

cards.question: Elihu isn't finished with Job yet. Who does Elihu say Job keeps company with?
According to Elihu, Job has said a man gets no profit from delighting in ___.

cards.text: So Elihu calls the men of understanding to listen up. Friend, THIS is the batch he's been preheating the oven for.

cards.question: Elihu says something is far from God and the Almighty. What is it?

answers.text: Hearing the cry of the poor

cards.question: Elihu says God repays a man according to his ___.

cards.text: Elihu hammers the point again: God does not act wickedly, and the Almighty does not pervert justice. Then he asks who gave God charge over the earth, and who appointed Him over the whole world.

cards.question: True or false: Elihu says that if God withdrew His Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish together.

cards.text: Elihu says, 'If you have understanding, hear this; listen to my words.' Then he asks whether one who hates justice could govern, and whether the listener will condemn the just and mighty One.

cards.question: True or false: Elihu says the just and mighty One goes easy on kings and nobles.
Elihu says God is not partial to princes and does not favor the rich over the poor. Why not?

answers.text: They are all the work of His hands
The poor pray more often than the rich
Riches never last for very long

cards.text: Elihu says the mighty die in an instant, in the middle of the night, removed without human hand, for God sees every step a man takes. Every step, baker? I don't even take steps, I hop around on this gold base, and I bet He counts every single hop.

cards.question: True or false: Elihu says the workers of iniquity can still hide from God in deep darkness.

cards.text: Elihu says God doesn't need to examine a man any further or bring him in for judgment. He shatters the mighty without inquiry.

cards.question: When God shatters the mighty, what else does Elihu say He does?

answers.text: Sets up others in their place
Hands their power to the poor

cards.text: Elihu says God recognizes their deeds and overthrows them in the night. He strikes them for their wickedness in full view.

cards.question: Elihu says God strikes the mighty for their wickedness. What reason does Elihu give?

answers.text: They grew too rich and proud

cards.question: Elihu says the mighty caused the cry of the ___ to come before God, and He heard the outcry of the ___.

cards.text: Then Elihu asks, 'But when He remains silent, who can condemn Him? When He hides His face, who can see Him?' Baker, I know quiet. Years in a junk drawer, and the loudest thing in there was a dust bunny landing.

cards.question: Even when God remains silent, what does Elihu say He still does?

answers.text: Rests from all of His work
Leaves the world to its kings

cards.question: True or false: Elihu says God watches over man and nation so that godless men should not rule.

cards.text: Then Elihu says suppose someone tells God, 'I have endured my punishment; I will offend no more. Teach me what I cannot see; if I have done wrong, I will not do it again.'
Elihu asks, 'Should God repay you on your own terms when you have disavowed Him?' Then he says somebody has to make a choice here.

cards.question: True or false: Elihu says he will be the one to make that choice.
Elihu says the wise men who hear him will speak up about Job. What does Elihu say they will say?

answers.text: Job has been wronged by God
Job is wiser than all of them

cards.text: Then Elihu says, 'If only Job were tried to the utmost for answering like a wicked man.' Oof. If words were ovens, baker, Elihu just cranked his all the way to broil.

cards.question: Elihu says Job adds ___ to his sin.

cards.text: Elihu says Job claps his hands among them and multiplies his words against God. And that's where we set the timer down for now, friend, because this story is far from finished.

findings.problem: The card states a Bible fact from outside the passage with no reference: that Elihu 'has been talking to Job' (Job 33). The Job 32:4, 6 references cover only the waiting.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: This story card tells no part of the passage. It is only a joke about Papa Dorin taste-testing, placed after Job 34:3 was already covered on card 2. That makes it a recap card that does not move the baker forward.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: Verse 20 says 'They die in an instant' and then separately 'the mighty are removed without human hand.' The text leaves open who 'They' are, and it follows verse 19's princes, rich and poor. The card merges the two lines into 'the mighty die in an instant,' which narrows what the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The two right answers, 'poor' and 'afflicted,' mean nearly the same thing in this line. A baker who puts 'afflicted' in blank 1 and 'poor' in blank 2 could argue they are right, but that order would be marked wrong.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The core action in verse 29 is that no one can condemn God when He stays silent or hides His face. The joke compares this to how quiet the junk drawer was, which is a different action. The joke also says the dust bunny was the loudest thing in the drawer. That contradicts the backstory, which has a rattling drawer, jingling batteries and batteries arguing.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The question says 'that choice,' which points back to story card 12. That card is no longer on screen, so the question doesn't say what the choice is.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The blank 'Job adds ___ to his sin' asks the baker to guess the wording of the line. Nothing on the earlier cards lets a baker reason to 'rebellion' over 'pride' or 'lies,' so the pick comes down to luck.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Many story cards are flat retellings with no Papa Dorin voice, such as stop 1 cards 5, 7, 14 and 16, and stop 2 cards 3, 5, 11 and 12. Together they read like a plain summary instead of the storyteller.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Two wrong answers here, 'Hearing the cry of the poor' and 'Watching over the nations,' are things God really does later in this passage (Job 34:28-29). 'Watches over man and nation' is the right answer on stop 2 card 9. A baker taught here that 'watching over the nations' is the wrong pick may be confused later.
findings.question: May a wrong answer be a statement that is true elsewhere in the passage when it is false as an answer to this question? Or should wrong answers avoid things the passage later presents as true about God?
